intro.html: Some hours crawl and some fly. This topic gives you words for both ends: for the things that bore us and the moods boredom brings, and for the things that grab our attention and won’t let go.

Boring things: tedious (long and tiresome), monotonous (the same, over and over). Bored people: indifferent (not caring), jaded (worn out by too much), blasé (unimpressed), and the feeling itself, ennui. Interested people: engrossed, rapt, intrigued. And the verb that starts it all: to pique someone’s interest.
Notice the difference between a thing and a person. A lecture is tedious; the student listening to it is bored or indifferent. A story is fascinating; the listener is rapt.

words.ex: Sorting a thousand buttons by color was a {tedious} job.
words.ctx: The first half of the movie was {tedious}, with long, slow scenes of people packing boxes, but the second half finally picked up speed.
words.etym: From Late Latin taediosus, from taedium (weariness, boredom).

mn.text: Sorting a hundred teddy bears by size takes hours and hours: the job is {tedious}.

scene.alt: A bored boy sits on the floor facing a huge pile of teddy bears to sort.

words.def: dull because it never changes; always the same
words.ex: The {monotonous} hum of the fan put the baby to sleep.
words.ctx: The speaker read every slide in the same flat, {monotonous} voice, never pausing or changing pitch, and half the audience was soon nodding off.
words.etym: From Greek monotonos, “of one tone”: monos (single) + tonos (tone).

mn.cue: MONO-TONE: one note, again and again
mn.text: Felix plays the same single piano key for an hour: “Plink… plink… plink…” The sound is {monotonous}.

scene.alt: A man plays the same piano key over and over while a woman yawns.

words.def: not caring or interested either way
words.ex: The cat seemed completely {indifferent} to its expensive new toy.
words.ctx: Most of the class cheered when the field trip was announced, but Dev seemed {indifferent}; he simply shrugged and went back to his drawing.
words.etym: From Latin indifferens, “making no difference”: in- (not) + differre (to differ).
words.note: Indifferent can also mean only average: an indifferent cook makes meals that are neither good nor bad.

mn.cue: it makes no DIFFERENCE to me
mn.text: Ask Uncle Marcus if he wants the red cup or the blue one, and he shrugs: it makes no difference to him. He is {indifferent}.

scene.alt: A girl offers a red cup or a blue one, and her uncle shrugs as if it makes no difference.

words.def: tired and bored from having too much of something
words.ex: After ten summers at the same beach, the {jaded} teenagers barely looked at the waves.
words.ctx: Having eaten at every fancy restaurant in the city, the critic had grown {jaded}; dishes that thrilled other diners only made her yawn.
words.etym: From jade, an old word for a worn-out horse.

mn.cue: a tired old JADE (a worn-out horse)
mn.text: An old word for a worn-out horse is a jade. Dusty has pulled the parade wagon a thousand times, and not even the brass band excites him now: he is {jaded}.

scene.alt: A bored old horse pulls a parade wagon past balloons and a drummer, not impressed at all.

words.def: unimpressed, as if one has seen it all before
words.ex: Kai acted {blasé} about meeting the star pitcher, but his hands were shaking.
words.ctx: First-time visitors gasped at the giant waterfall, but the park ranger, who saw it every day, was {blasé} and kept checking her watch.
words.etym: From French blasé, “worn out by too much pleasure,” from blaser (to wear out).

mn.text: The fireworks burst in every color, and little Ivy squeals, but her big sister just says, “Blah.” Rosa is {blasé}.

scene.alt: Under bursting fireworks, a little girl cheers while her teen sister crosses her arms and says, “Blah.”

words.def: a weary, restless feeling of boredom
words.ex: By the fourth rainy afternoon, a heavy {ennui} had settled over the cabin.
words.ctx: Despite having every toy and game he could want, the young prince suffered from {ennui}; nothing excited him, and the long days dragged by.

mn.text: On the tenth rainy day of summer, the cousins sigh on the sofa: “What do WE do now?” They are full of {ennui}.

scene.alt: Two bored cousins slump in the living room on a rainy day, with nothing to do.

words.def: so interested that one notices nothing else
words.ex: Maya was so {engrossed} in her puzzle that she forgot to eat lunch.
words.ctx: The scientist was {engrossed} in her experiment; she did not hear the phone, the doorbell or her assistant calling her name.

mn.cue: so lost in it, she misses the GROSS frog
mn.text: Lila is so deep in her book that she never notices the gross, slimy frog sitting on her head: she is {engrossed}.

scene.alt: A girl reads happily, not noticing the frog sitting on top of her head.

words.ex: The children listened in {rapt} silence as Grandpa told the story of the winter the river froze solid.
words.ctx: The audience sat {rapt} through the whole concert; no one coughed, whispered or checked a phone until the final note faded.
words.etym: From Latin raptus, “seized, carried away,” from rapere (to seize).

mn.text: The children sit wrapped up in Professor Edwin’s tale, mouths open, not moving a muscle: they are {rapt}.

scene.alt: Three children sit on the floor, spellbound, as an old professor reads them a story.

words.def: very curious and eager to know more
words.ex: Lila was {intrigued} by the old map she found in the attic.
words.ctx: At first the detective thought the case was simple, but the muddy footprints that led nowhere left her {intrigued}, and she spent all night studying them.
words.etym: From French intriguer, “to puzzle,” from Italian intrigare (to tangle).

mn.text: A locked box sits high in the old oak tree. Who put it there, and what is inside? Kai can’t stop wondering: he is {intrigued}.

scene.alt: A boy points up at a mysterious locked chest wedged high in a tree.

words.def: to stir up interest or curiosity
words.ex: The movie trailer was made to {pique} your curiosity without giving away the ending.
words.ctx: The museum hoped the giant dinosaur skeleton in the lobby would {pique} visitors’ interest and draw them deeper into the exhibits.
words.note: As a noun, pique means a flash of hurt pride or annoyance: she left in a fit of pique.

mn.text: Through a knothole in the fence, Zoe takes one peek at the new neighbor’s puppy, and that peek {piques} her curiosity.

scene.alt: A girl on tiptoe peeks over a fence at a puppy, suddenly curious.

head: describes
bored side

after.cap: Match the word to what it describes: the thing, the person or the feeling.

after.html: You pique someone’s interest: you stir it up. You do not “peak” it (reach the top) or “peek” it (glance). The three words sound the same, which is why the hook above uses a peek to remember the spelling of the one that stirs.

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: The mystery in chapter one was meant to {pique} the reader’s curiosity.

after.cap: To stir curiosity is to pique it.

items.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The strange noise in the attic ______ my curiosity.”
items.why: Piqued means stirred up. Peaked means reached the top, and peeked means glanced.

items.q: The diner’s food was indifferent: not bad, not good. Here indifferent means…
items.why: Besides not caring, indifferent can mean mediocre, neither good nor bad.

items.q: True or false: a rapt audience is paying close attention.
items.why: True. Rapt means completely fascinated, as if wrapped up in what is happening.

items.q: Copying a phone book by hand would be…
items.why: A long, dull task is tedious. Intrigued, rapt and blasé describe how people feel, not tasks.
